segments.narration: This weapon burned on water and nobody can rebuild it. Constantinople, the 670s. Fire pumped from bronze tubes on the prows of warships. Seawater did not touch it.
A refugee architect called Kallinikos brought it to the emperor around 672. Arab fleets at the walls caught light and kept burning.
Seven centuries of use, and not one usable recipe survives. Why? Because no single operator was ever told the whole system.
Bulgarians captured 36 of the tubes and a stock of the substance in 814. They never managed to fire any of it.
Scholars now read it as petroleum thickened with resin. A full-scale rebuild in 2002 threw flame fifteen metres, above a thousand degrees.

verdicts.claim: Byzantine Greek fire burned on water and was projected through bronze tubes called siphons mounted on warships, especially near the prow.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: the main method was projection through a tube called a siphon mounted on ships, especially near the prow, and it burned on water; the World History Encyclopedia gives spraying under pressure from bronze tubes with a siphon pump and swivelling nozzle, and says water had no effect on it.

verdicts.claim: Theophanes the Confessor credits Greek fire to Kallinikos, an architect who fled to the Romans, around 672, and it was used against Arab fleets at the siege of Constantinople of 674-678.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia dates development to c. 672, credited by Theophanes the Confessor to Kallinikos, an architect who fled to the Romans, and gives first use at the siege of Constantinople of 674-678 against Arab fleets. The World History Encyclopedia dates first use to 678 CE in that siege, so the narration says 'the 670s'.

verdicts.claim: Knowledge of Greek fire was compartmentalised as a state secret, so no single operator knew the whole system, and the composition was eventually lost.
verdicts.note: 86% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: The Bulgarians captured 36 siphons and a quantity of the substance in 814 and were unable to use them.
verdicts.note: 88% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Most modern scholars hold that Greek fire was petroleum-based with added resins, and John Haldon's 2002 full-scale test with crude oil and wood resins produced a flame above 1,000 degrees Celsius with a range of up to 15 metres.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia records the modern scholarly consensus of a petroleum base mixed with resins, comparable to napalm, and Haldon's 2002 full-scale test reaching a flame temperature above 1,000 C with a range of up to 15 metres using crude oil and wood resins. The World History Encyclopedia gives 10-15 metres for a Haldon replica, so fifteen metres is the upper figure both report.
